questions.scenario: A team needs to benchmark 4 candidate FMs across 5,000 custom prompts on subjective writing quality. Hiring human raters is too slow and expensive; standard metrics like BLEU don't fit because there is no single reference output.
questions.stem: Which Bedrock Model Evaluation job type is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Automated evaluation with built-in datasets only.
options.why: Built-in datasets don't match the team's custom prompts; standard metrics like BLEU don't fit subjective quality.

options.text: Human evaluation with an in-house team.
options.why: Too slow and expensive at 5,000 prompts × 4 models.

options.text: LLM-as-a-judge evaluation in Bedrock Model Evaluation.
options.why: Uses another FM (e.g., Claude or Nova) to score subjective qualities at scale — faster and cheaper than human raters, with documented metrics.

options.text: Skip evaluation and choose by gut feel.
options.why: Not a valid engineering answer.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock Model Evaluation job types: Automated (built-in/custom datasets, standard metrics), Human (your team, custom criteria), LLM-as-a-Judge (FM scores at scale, faster than human).
questions.trap_alert: Don't pick Human eval when 'scale + speed + cost' all matter. LLM-as-a-Judge is the scale answer.

questions.scenario: A team evaluates a summarization model with built-in metrics.
questions.stem: Which metric is MOST appropriate for summarization quality?

options.why: BLEU is traditionally for machine TRANSLATION (precision of n-gram matches).
ROUGE is the canonical RECALL-oriented metric family for summarization — measures n-gram overlap with reference summaries.
Perplexity measures model confidence on a held-out set; not a summarization-quality task metric.
Strict equality is unrealistic for summarization.

questions.knowledge_point: Metric ↔ task: BLEU=translation; ROUGE=summarization; BERTScore=semantic similarity; F1/Exact Match=classification/QA; Perplexity=LM confidence.
questions.trap_alert: BLEU vs ROUGE is a frequent swap-trap. Don't pick BLEU for summarization.

questions.scenario: A RAG application's accuracy depends on whether the right chunks are in the top-K retrieved results. The team needs a metric that captures whether the gold-standard chunk appears within the top-K results.
questions.stem: Which retrieval metric is MOST appropriate?

options.why: Recall@K is exactly 'is the gold chunk in the top-K returned'. Canonical retrieval recall measure.
BLEU is for translation, not retrieval ranking.
Perplexity measures LM uncertainty, not retrieval quality.
Doesn't measure ranking; only equality of full string.

questions.knowledge_point: RAG retrieval metrics: Recall@K (gold in top-K), Precision@K (fraction of top-K that's relevant), MRR (Mean Reciprocal Rank of first relevant), NDCG (graded relevance with position discount), Hit Rate.
questions.trap_alert: Retrieval metrics ≠ generation metrics. Don't pick BLEU/ROUGE for retrieval quality.

questions.scenario: A team must alarm when Bedrock model invocation client errors (4xx) spike for the Claude 3 Sonnet model.
questions.stem: Which CloudWatch metric is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Bedrock InvocationClientErrors metric, dimensioned by model.
options.why: CloudWatch publishes Bedrock metrics including InvocationClientErrors per model — alarmable directly.
That's a Lambda-side metric and would only catch errors at the Lambda layer.
Concurrency, not errors.
API Gateway-side; doesn't reflect Bedrock-side 4xx behavior.

questions.knowledge_point: Bedrock CloudWatch metrics: Invocations, InputTokenCount, OutputTokenCount, InvocationLatency, InvocationThrottles, InvocationClientErrors, InvocationServerErrors. Dimension by model.
questions.trap_alert: Pick the BEDROCK service metric, not the proxy-layer (Lambda / API Gateway) metric.

questions.scenario: Production logs show frequent ThrottlingException (429) errors on Claude 3 Sonnet invocations during business hours.
questions.stem: Which is the MOST APPROPRIATE first action?

options.text: Add exponential backoff with jitter on 429, then evaluate Service Quotas for TPM/RPM increase or use a cross-region inference profile.
options.why: Standard pattern: absorb transient throttles with backoff+jitter; then address ceiling with quota increase or cross-region capacity.
Unrelated to throttling.

options.text: Switch model family to a different vendor without analysis.
options.why: Knee-jerk; doesn't solve the actual capacity ceiling.
Per-call cap, not a capacity setting.

questions.knowledge_point: 429 troubleshooting playbook: backoff with jitter → Service Quotas request → cross-region inference profile → Provisioned Throughput for sustained loads.
questions.trap_alert: Backoff alone is insufficient if the workload genuinely exceeds quotas. Need a structural fix.

questions.scenario: A RAG pipeline occasionally returns answers not actually supported by retrieved chunks. The team needs to flag and reject low-grounded responses automatically at runtime.

options.text: Bedrock Guardrails Contextual Grounding check applied to each response.
options.why: Native runtime grounding check: scores groundedness/relevance and can block on threshold. The runtime tool for this signature.
RAGAS is useful for OFFLINE evaluation; doesn't reject low-grounded responses at runtime.

options.text: Increase temperature so the model says 'I don't know'.
options.why: Higher temperature INCREASES variability; doesn't enforce grounding.
Fine-tuning doesn't reliably reduce hallucinations on changing facts.

questions.knowledge_point: Runtime hallucination rejection on RAG = Contextual Grounding (groundedness threshold + relevance threshold). RAGAS = offline RAG evaluation framework.
questions.trap_alert: Runtime vs offline matters. Pick Contextual Grounding for runtime; RAGAS for offline batch evaluation.

questions.scenario: A product team wants to ship a new model variant to 10% of users and compare quality metrics versus the existing model.
questions.stem: Which pattern MOST appropriately implements this?

options.text: A/B test via traffic-splitting at the application layer (or via SageMaker variant traffic shifting); collect outcome metrics into CloudWatch / S3 and compare.
options.why: Standard A/B test pattern: deterministic split, collect metrics, compare. App-layer routing is the simplest path.

options.text: Replace the model for all users immediately and review next quarter.
options.why: Big-bang switch contradicts the gradual-evaluation intent.

options.text: Use Bedrock Knowledge Bases to A/B test.
options.why: KBs don't do model variant traffic splitting.

options.text: Disable model invocation logging during the test.
options.why: Logging is needed to measure outcomes.

questions.knowledge_point: A/B testing patterns: app-layer split with deterministic hash on user_id, log outcomes, compare. For SageMaker-hosted models, variant traffic shifting is built in.
questions.trap_alert: Don't pick KBs or Guardrails as A/B mechanisms — they don't split traffic.

questions.scenario: A team wants to evaluate a new model on real production traffic without serving its responses to users.

options.text: Shadow testing — mirror requests to the new model in parallel, but only the existing model's response is returned to the user.
options.why: Shadow testing is exactly this pattern: zero user impact, real-traffic comparison.
Canary serves some real users with the new variant — user impact is non-zero.
Atomic cutover, also impacts users on cutover.
Inject failures, unrelated to model comparison.

questions.knowledge_point: Shadow testing = mirror traffic, evaluate silently. Canary = small % real users. Blue/green = atomic cutover. Pick by user-impact tolerance.
questions.trap_alert: Canary and shadow both reduce risk but at different tolerance levels. Shadow has zero user impact.

questions.scenario: Production users occasionally trigger a ValidationException with message indicating the prompt exceeds the model's context window.

options.text: Truncate or chunk long inputs, retrieve only top-K most relevant chunks via RAG, and pre-validate token count before InvokeModel.
options.why: Three-layer defense: chunk + retrieve + pre-validate. Cleanest production pattern for context-window issues.
max_tokens is OUTPUT cap, not input window.
Unrelated to context length.
Throughput model doesn't change context-window limits.

questions.knowledge_point: Context window exceeded → reduce input size (truncate/chunk/RAG) + pre-validate token count client-side using a tokenizer.
questions.trap_alert: max_tokens controls OUTPUT, not INPUT. Don't confuse the two when chasing context-window errors.

questions.scenario: A SageMaker-hosted fine-tuned model needs continuous monitoring for data quality drift, model quality drift, and bias drift.
questions.stem: Which AWS service is MOST appropriate?

options.why: Model Monitor detects four drift types — data quality, model quality, bias, and feature attribution drift — on SageMaker endpoints.
RUM is for real-user monitoring of web/mobile apps.
Config tracks AWS resource configuration, not model performance.
Distributed tracing, not model drift.

questions.knowledge_point: SageMaker Model Monitor: four drift types — data quality, model quality, bias, feature attribution. For Bedrock-only GenAI workloads, build custom CloudWatch metrics + scheduled Model Evaluation jobs.
questions.trap_alert: Model Monitor is SageMaker-specific. Bedrock-only workloads need a custom pipeline of metrics + scheduled evals.

questions.scenario: A team wants the latest production model to be re-evaluated weekly against a frozen test set, with results stored for trend analysis.
questions.stem: Which AWS-native architecture is MOST appropriate?

options.text: EventBridge schedule → Lambda → start a Bedrock Model Evaluation job → results saved to S3 → Athena/QuickSight for trend dashboards.
options.why: EventBridge schedule + Lambda + Bedrock Eval is the canonical AWS-native continuous-evaluation pipeline.

options.text: Run a manual evaluation every Monday morning.
options.why: Manual = not continuous.
Config doesn't run model evaluations.
Macie is for sensitive-data discovery.

questions.knowledge_point: Continuous evaluation pattern: EventBridge (schedule) → Lambda (orchestrator) → Bedrock Evaluation → S3 (results) → Athena/QuickSight (dashboards).
questions.trap_alert: EventBridge is the missing piece many forget — it's the AWS-native scheduler.

questions.scenario: An engineer is debugging why a Bedrock Agent chose to call a particular action group when a different one was expected. They need to see the FM's intermediate reasoning and tool-selection decisions.

options.text: Bedrock Agent trace — captures rationale, orchestration steps, tool invocations, and KB retrievals per InvokeAgent call.
options.why: Agent trace is the debugging mechanism showing the orchestrator's reasoning step by step.
CloudTrail audits API calls, not the FM's reasoning.
Network-layer; no reasoning info.
Distributed tracing, not Agent reasoning capture.

questions.knowledge_point: Agent trace = FM rationale + steps + tool calls + KB hits per invocation. Use for production Agent debugging.
questions.trap_alert: Agent trace ≠ CloudTrail ≠ X-Ray. Each captures a different layer.

questions.stem: Which combinations of task and metric are CORRECT? (Select TWO)

options.why: BLEU was originally designed for and remains canonical for MT n-gram precision.
ROUGE is the standard recall-oriented metric family for summarization.
BLEU is generation; classification uses F1, Accuracy, AUC.
Retrieval uses Recall@K, Precision@K, MRR, NDCG.
Image gen uses FID, CLIPScore — not perplexity.

questions.knowledge_point: Task → metric: Translation/BLEU; Summarization/ROUGE; Classification/F1; Retrieval/Recall@K, MRR, NDCG; Semantic similarity/BERTScore; LM perplexity for LM uncertainty.
questions.trap_alert: Mismatch task-and-metric is the #1 metric trap. Memorize the mappings cold.

questions.scenario: A team needs to analyze WHY specific user prompts were blocked by Guardrails over a 30-day window.
questions.stem: Where is the trace data persisted for retroactive analysis?

options.text: Enable Bedrock model invocation logging — Guardrail traces are included in the logged events stored in S3 or CloudWatch.
options.why: Guardrail traces are emitted as part of model invocation logs; persisted via the logging destination for retroactive analysis.
Config does not store per-invocation traces.
Macie discovers PII in S3; unrelated to Guardrail traces.
Network metadata only.

questions.knowledge_point: Guardrail traces live inside model invocation logs (S3/CloudWatch). Enable invocation logging to retain traces; query via Athena or CloudWatch Logs Insights.
questions.trap_alert: Don't expect a separate 'Guardrail log' product — it's embedded in model invocation logs.

questions.scenario: p99 latency on InvokeModel calls to Claude 3 Sonnet has gradually climbed over a month. CloudWatch shows no throttles, no error increase, and token counts per request are unchanged.
questions.stem: Which is the MOST LIKELY NEXT investigation step?

options.text: Check whether requests are being routed via a cross-region inference profile and whether one of the routed regions is degraded.
options.why: Cross-region inference can route to a region with degraded latency; this is a known investigation lever when no other CloudWatch dimension explains the drift.
Removes a feature without evidence Guardrails caused the drift.

options.text: Switch to On-Demand from Provisioned Throughput.
options.why: Premature without root cause analysis.
Unrelated to latency.

questions.knowledge_point: Latency drift root-cause checklist: cross-region inference health, region of execution, network path (PrivateLink vs internet), model version changes, prompt-size drift, output length drift, downstream Lambda cold-starts.
questions.trap_alert: Don't change capacity model or remove safety features without evidence. Investigate routing first.
